processing: Steamed and rolled mountain sencha, made in the usual Japanese way; matured tea from a mountain tea store is also made.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other Shizuoka mountain teas, with the first picking prized.
appearance_dry: Typically slim, dark green needles of a lightly steamed mountain sencha.
appearance_wet: Mostly intact green leaf, as is usual for a lighter steaming.
taste_profile: Described as a premium mountain tea; expect the clean aroma and fresh, lightly brisk sweetness typical of Shizuoka's high valley senchas.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a lightly steamed sencha. Cooler water keeps the mountain aroma and holds back astringency.

vintage_note: Sold mainly as the current year's spring tea, with new-crop lots the most valued. A matured version, kept in a mountain tea store, is also made.
description:
Honyama-cha is the mountain tea of Shizuoka City, grown in the upper valleys of the Abe river and its tributary the Warashina. It is known as a leading high-grade Shizuoka brand, and it has one of the strongest claims in the prefecture to being where it all started.

The tea is steamed and rolled sencha made in the ordinary way; what sets it apart is place. Shizuoka's upriver gardens are generally thought to give high-quality leaf, helped by cool, misty conditions.

Expect what is typical of Shizuoka mountain sencha: clear colour, a clean aroma and a brisk edge under the sweetness. Use water around 75 C and do not oversteep.

When buying, look for the valley or the district. Tea from Ashikubo may be sold under its own name, Ashikubo-cha. New-crop spring lots are the main event, though a matured version kept in a mountain store is also made.
history:
By tradition, tea in Shizuoka starts here: the monk Shoichi Kokushi (Enni Benen), born about 800 years ago in what is now Tochisawa, is said to have planted seed brought from Song China at Ashikubo. Treat it as tradition. The later story that Tokugawa Ieyasu loved Ashikubo tea is told in the same spirit.

The tea was long called Abe-cha. To set it apart from other areas it was renamed Honyama-cha, reportedly in the Taisho period, by a local tea man who helped build up the district. It was also presented to Emperor Meiji.
